newsitem.title: BELARUS: High poll points to Lukashenko win in Belarus.
newsitem.headline: High poll points to Lukashenko win in Belarus.

text.p: A high poll in a controversial referendum in Belarus appeared to point to victory for hardline President Alexander Lukashenko's plans to rewrite the country's constitution as overnight counting got under way on Monday.
Officials, speaking after the 6,500 polling stations closed at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) on Sunday, said the turnout was likely to top 84 percent, Russia's Itar-Tass news agency reported.

Interfax news agency quoted sources in Lukashenko's administration as saying more than 6.1 million votes were cast and most backed the president, who wants to widen his powers and extend his term beyond 2000.

At least half of the registered 7.2 million voters have to say yes to Lukashenko's new constitution, one of seven questions on the complex ballot paper, for him to claim victory. Voting began on November 9.

Lukashenko, 42, scheduled a mid-morning news conference and appeared confident of trouncing his parliamentary opponents after a one-sided campaign in which he monopolised the media and sacked the head of the electoral commission.
He told voters they lived in "a small island of order and stability in an ocean of chaos and anarchy" which covered the rest of the former Soviet Union.
A small delegation from the European parliament arrived in Minsk at the invitation of parliament speaker Semyon Sharetsky to monitor the overnight count.

But its leader Herbert Bosch told Reuters it was unlikely to be granted access because it had failed to seek accreditation in advance. "We did not seek accreditation because it would have gone too far in terms of validating the referendum," he said.

Lukashenko has ignored Western criticism of his increasingly authoritarian rule under which the media have been gagged, free trade unions banned and leading nationalist opponents have fled into exile.

Several hundred people demonstrated in Minsk against Lukashenko on polling day but the capital was otherwise calm, reflecting Lukashenko's control over the security apparatus and the lack of strong opposition leadership in the republic of 10 million bordering Russia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Ukraine.

Rural voters in Belarussia's thousands of villages looked certain to give their support to Lukashenko's plans to rewrite the constitution to extend his term in office and extend his control over rival institutions.

However, the president, in genial mood as he voted on Sunday, ruled out any immediate move to dissolve parliament, whose leaders have fought a rearguard battle to thwart his plans which they have denounced as dictatorship.

Moves are still pending by deputies to remove Lukashenko from office, but his determination to ignore decisions by parliament and the constitutional court is likely to be strengthened if the voting goes his way.
Lukashenko has insisted that the referendum should be mandatory rather than consultative, effectively closing the door to further debate on constitutional reform.
The outcome of the poll was being closely watched in Russia, which brokered a compromise between Lukashenko and parliament on Friday which collapsed after less than a day.

Lukashenko, the most pro-Russian of all leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States, has effectively blunted criticism from Moscow of his policies by identifying himself as the guarantor of closer integration between the two states.
Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin expressed "deep regret" on Sunday over the collapse of the compromise he arranged and blamed some legislators for wrecking the truce.
But the Russian premier told Itar-Tass news agency that Lukashenko could also have done more to make it succeed.
The tall, angular, moustachioed Lukashenko was in conciliatory mood on Sunday about his opponents in parliament.
"The new constitution allows me to dissolve parliament after a month if we do not reach agreement," he said, but added: "I will not dissolve it because we will find harmony."
